Hard times

Feeling that you are wasting your time

The feeling that life is slipping away between chores and screens is very common. What causes it and how to reclaim the time that matters.

"I don't know where the year went." It is a common phrase, and behind it there is usually an uncomfortable feeling: that the days pass full of things but empty of what really matters. Almost two thousand years ago, the philosopher Seneca wrote in On the Shortness of Life that life is not short, but that we waste much of it.

Why time seems to fly

Our sense of time depends on what we remember. Routine weeks leave few distinct memories and, looking back, seem to have passed very quickly. New experiences, by contrast, leave many traces and lengthen the memory of that period. That is why a holiday somewhere new seems long when you remember it.

A mind that is not where we are

In a 2010 study of thousands of people who were asked by phone what they were doing and thinking about, Matthew Killingsworth and Daniel Gilbert found that the mind was elsewhere almost half the time, and that people were less happy when their mind wandered. Add to that unintended phone use: short stretches that add up to hours and leave little memory or satisfaction.

Time poverty

Many people feel they never have time, even though their free hours have not decreased. Ashley Whillans and colleagues showed that spending some money to buy time, for example paying for disliked chores, was associated with more wellbeing than spending it on material things. The sense of having time depends as much on how it is used as on how much there is.

What tends to help

  • Tracking where time goes for a week, without judging, to see what matches what matters and what does not.
  • Protecting time for what is important, such as relationships, rest or a hobby, just as you would book a medical appointment.
  • Bringing novelty into routine: a different route, a different plan at the weekend.
  • Using your phone with intention, switching off notifications and keeping it away at certain times of day.
  • Accepting some "wasted" time. Resting or being bored also has value; not everything has to be productive.

References

  1. Séneca (c. 49 d. C.). De brevitate vitae [Sobre la brevedad de la vida].
  2. Killingsworth, M. A. y Gilbert, D. T. (2010). A wandering mind is an unhappy mind. Science, 330, 932.
  3. Whillans, A. V. et al. (2017). Buying time promotes happiness. PNAS, 114(32), 8523–8527.
  4. Wittmann, M. (2016). Felt Time: The Psychology of How We Perceive Time. Cambridge (MA): MIT Press.
